language.name: French
features: Simple statements use subject + verb + complement.
Prefix a statement with est-ce que for a predictable yes/no question.
Written negation uses ne/n’ before the verb and pas after it.
Je contracts to j’ before a vowel: j’ai, but je n’ai.
Needing something uses avoir besoin de, not a direct cognate of need.

lessons.title: First words
lessons.goal: Start and end a simple interaction
lessons.introduction: A few social expressions are conventional, not assembled by grammar. Learn these short forms as complete units.

notes.explanation: Treat greetings and politeness formulas as ready-made expressions. They do not require verb conjugation study to be useful.
notes.detail: Bonjour works for a general daytime hello and good morning. This guide uses vous with people you do not know.
notes.caution: French social conventions often favor a greeting before asking a question in a shop or office.

lessons.title: Needs and possession
lessons.goal: Say what you need or already have
lessons.introduction: A verb plus an interchangeable noun phrase gives you a whole family of useful statements.

notes.recipe: J’ai besoin de + noun. / J’ai + noun.
notes.explanation: French expresses “need” with the construction avoir besoin de: literally, “have need of.” J’ai is the “I have” form.
notes.detail: De changes form before vowels: d’eau, d’aide. Learn j’ai besoin d’eau and j’ai besoin d’un billet as complete examples.
notes.caution: Never translate English “I need” word for word as a simple invented verb conjugation.

lessons.title: What you would like
lessons.introduction: One courteous construction works with many objects. Substitute the thing you want instead of memorizing an order.

notes.explanation: Je voudrais is a polite, practical way to order or request something. It is softer than je veux.
notes.detail: For example, un café and un billet take un, while water is de l’eau. A formal question to another person starts Est-ce que vous voudriez … ?
notes.caution: Je veux can sound overly forceful when ordering. Learn je voudrais as a complete reusable pattern.

examples.target: Est-ce que vous voudriez un café ?
Est-ce que vous voudriez de l’eau ?

lessons.title: Yes/no questions
lessons.introduction: A question changes the form of a whole clause. The same mechanism works with several verbs.

notes.explanation: Put est-ce que before a statement to turn it into a yes/no question. The original subject–verb order stays the same.
notes.detail: Est-ce que vous avez le temps ? is predictable and understandable. Spoken French also uses rising intonation, but this guide teaches one written form.
notes.caution: Formal written French adds a space before ? and other high punctuation; the examples follow that convention.

examples.target: Est-ce que vous avez le temps ?
Est-ce que vous avez un billet ?

lessons.title: Ask for help
lessons.introduction: A question, a modal verb and an action can be combined. Change the recipient or action to make a new request.

notes.recipe: Est-ce que vous pouvez + infinitive, s’il vous plaît ?
notes.explanation: Vous pouvez means “you can.” Add an infinitive such as aider or répéter. Add s’il vous plaît for a courteous request.
notes.detail: French object pronouns attach to the verb phrase: vous pouvez m’aider, and vous m’aidez without a modal. The word order differs from German.
notes.caution: The pronoun goes before the infinitive in m’aider; it is not a separate noun after aider.

examples.target: Est-ce que vous pouvez m’aider, s’il vous plaît ?
Est-ce que vous pouvez répéter ça, s’il vous plaît ?

lessons.title: When you do not understand
lessons.introduction: Say what you cannot understand and ask for clarification instead of trying to guess.

notes.recipe: Je ne comprends pas. / Parlez lentement, s’il vous plaît.
notes.explanation: Formal negation surrounds the finite verb with ne … pas. The polite imperative is easier to memorize as a fixed chunk.
notes.detail: Before a vowel, ne contracts to n’: je n’ai pas. Je becomes j’ before a vowel, but not before ne.
notes.caution: In conversation some speakers omit ne. This guide uses complete standard written forms for consistency.

lessons.title: Places and directions
lessons.goal: Find a place and say where you are going
lessons.introduction: The place is a slot. Its preposition and article are handled by the language, not by you inventing a new sentence.

notes.recipe: Où est + place ? / Je vais + destination.
notes.explanation: Où est asks where something is. French destinations use different prepositions and articles.
notes.detail: Learn à la gare, à l’hôtel, aux toilettes and chez moi as chunks. The bathroom question is plural: Où sont les toilettes ?
notes.caution: Do not use où est with toilettes: the standard form uses the plural verb sont.

lessons.title: Buying and paying
lessons.goal: Ask a price and pay for something
lessons.introduction: Combine price questions, purchasing and payment methods. Only the useful noun or payment method changes.

notes.recipe: Combien coûte + noun ? / Je peux payer par carte ?
notes.explanation: Combien coûte asks a price. Payer par carte is the common construction for paying by card.
notes.detail: You can ask Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ? and respond je paie en espèces. These use the same can + infinitive pattern.
notes.caution: Café and billet take un as singular count nouns; water normally uses de l’eau.

examples.english: How much does a ticket cost?
How much does a coffee cost?
I want to buy a ticket.
I want to buy a coffee.

examples.target: Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?
Est-ce que je peux payer en espèces ?

lessons.title: Today and tomorrow
lessons.goal: Situate a simple statement in time
lessons.introduction: Adding a time expression makes ordinary statements useful for near-future plans, without learning new tenses first.

notes.explanation: Aujourd’hui means today, demain means tomorrow. In these simple clauses, the time expression typically appears at the end.
notes.detail: The near future can often be conveyed by the present tense plus demain. This is a restricted learning recipe, not a complete tense system.
notes.caution: The apostrophe in aujourd’hui is part of the spelling.

examples.english: I go to the hotel tomorrow.
I go to the station tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais à la gare demain.
Est-ce que vous pouvez m’aider demain ?

examples.english: I want to buy a ticket today.
examples.target: Je veux acheter un billet aujourd’hui.

lessons.title: Say no and set limits
lessons.goal: Turn a positive sentence into a negative one
lessons.introduction: Negation is an operator: it changes the meaning of a clause, while each language decides where its negative words go.

notes.explanation: To make a sentence negative, wrap the finite verb in ne … pas. With a vowel sound the first part becomes n’.
notes.detail: Compare j’ai un billet with je n’ai pas de billet. French often changes un to de after negated avoir.
notes.caution: A negative modal puts pas after the modal: je ne peux pas aller, not after aller.

examples.english: I do not have a ticket.
I cannot go to the station today.
examples.target: Je ne peux pas aller à la gare aujourd’hui.

lessons.title: Put the blocks together
lessons.introduction: Put a greeting, a question, a need and a request into separate short sentences. Complexity is optional.

notes.recipe: Excusez-moi. → Où est … ? → J’ai besoin de … → Merci.
notes.explanation: Build an interaction from short, complete requests. Make one request at a time rather than joining everything into one sentence.
notes.detail: Start with bonjour in shops, use vous and s’il vous plaît for formal courtesy, and keep your question structure consistent.
notes.caution: Real conversations include replies and informal variants beyond this intentionally small production subset.

examples.english: How much does a ticket cost?

examples.target: Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?
